content_units: Slow Kitchen Drain: Most Likely Scenario
Given your facts, this is   most likely a localized kitchen drain restriction  , not a whole-apartment sewer problem.

Because the   bathroom drains are normal   and there is   no sewage odor  , the blockage is probably in the   kitchen sink trap, branch line, or grease buildup near the sink  , rather than in the main drain stack.
Most Probable Causes
Cause   Why it fits your symptoms   Likelihood   First safe check
Grease, oil, and soap residue buildup   Causes gradual narrowing over weeks/months; common in kitchen-only slow drains   High   Flush with hot water + dish soap, then inspect trap if accessible

Food particles collecting in trap or branch pipe   No disposal installed means scraps may still enter drain; partial blockage slows but does not fully stop flow   High   Remove and clean sink strainer; check trap
Sink trap sludge   Traps collect fatty residue, coffee grounds, starch, and sediment   High   Place bucket under trap and clean it

Minor venting issue affecting kitchen line   Can slow drainage without full blockage, though less likely if only worsening gradually   Medium   Listen for gurgling; note whether draining improves when faucet runs slowly
Pipe scale or old residue in branch line   Older apartment plumbing can accumulate narrowing inside the pipe   Medium   Use a hand drain snake after trap cleaning
Misuse items in drain (coffee grounds, rice, flour, eggshells)   These can form paste-like buildup over time   Medium   Review habits and clear trap/line
Safe Troubleshooting Checklist
Step   Action   What to Check   Expected Result
1   Boil water, add a little dish soap, flush in 2-3 stages   Only if pipes are metal or standard kitchen waste line; avoid if fragile old PVC is suspected   Light grease may soften and flow better
2   Clean sink strainer and visible drain opening   Remove slime, food debris, grease film   Water should enter opening more freely
3   Use a sink plunger with overflow sealed if present   Add some water to basin for seal   Partial blockage may loosen
4   Clean the P-trap under the sink   Put bucket and towels below; remove sludge and rinse   Often restores normal flow immediately
5   Use a hand drain snake or zip tool into the branch line   Feed beyond trap, rotate gently, pull debris out   Removes soft clogs deeper in line
6   Re-test with a full sink of water   Watch whether drain speed improves and whether leaks appear under sink   Confirms if obstruction is mostly cleared
Practical Step-by-Step Plan
1) Start with the safest low-effort fix
- Pour a small amount of   dish soap   into the drain.
- Follow with   hot water   in stages, not one giant dump.
- Wait 5-10 minutes and test drainage.
2) Try plunging
- Use a   cup plunger   on the kitchen sink.
- If you have a double sink,   seal the other side   with a stopper or wet cloth.
- Pump firmly 15-20 times, then test.
3) Clean the trap
- Put a bucket under the   P-trap  .
- Unscrew slip nuts if accessible by hand or pliers.
- Remove grease sludge, rinse the trap, reinstall, then run water.
4) Snake the line
- Use a   manual drain snake  , not a powered auger.
- Insert past the trap into the wall-side pipe.
- Rotate gently and pull back debris.
5) Recheck drainage behavior
- Fill the sink halfway and release.
- If it improves but is still slow, buildup likely remains deeper in the branch line.
- If unchanged, professional cleaning may be more efficient.
What Not to Do
-   Do not use harsh chemical drain cleaners   if you want to avoid them; they can damage pipes, create splash hazards, and make later trap cleaning unpleasant.
-   Do not mix cleaners   of any kind.
-   Do not pour boiling water repeatedly into suspect old plastic fittings   if you are unsure of pipe condition.
-   Do not use excessive force with a snake  ; it can damage trap fittings or push a soft clog tighter.
-   Do not keep flushing grease with hot water alone   as a long-term solution; it often just moves the clog farther down.
-   Do not put these down the kitchen drain:   oil, fat, coffee grounds, rice, pasta, flour, eggshells, fibrous vegetable scraps.
When a Plumber Becomes Necessary
You should move to professional service if any of these apply:
- The drain is   still slow after trap cleaning and hand snaking  .
- Water begins to   back up quickly   or the sink becomes nearly blocked.
- You hear   repeated gurgling   from the sink or nearby pipes.
- You find   leaks under the sink   after reassembly.
- The problem keeps returning within days or a couple of weeks.
- More fixtures later become slow, which may indicate a   shared branch or stack issue  .
- You live in an older building and suspect   pipe scale, hardened grease, or line configuration issues  .
Best-Fit Conclusion for Your Apartment
For your 70 m² apartment, the pattern points most strongly to   gradual grease/food sludge buildup in the kitchen trap or kitchen branch drain  .

The best first moves are:   clean the strainer, plunge, remove and clean the P-trap, then use a manual snake  . If that does not substantially improve flow, a plumber will likely need to   mechanically clear the kitchen branch line  .
